title: Personality Tests: Projective and Objective
summary: Projective personality tests; objective personality inventories; major tests and their features; administration and scoring; clinical applications.
objectives: Distinguish projective from objective personality tests.
Describe Rorschach, TAT, Rosenzweig and Szondi.
Describe 16PF, NEO-PI-3, EPQ-R, MBTI, MMPI, MCMI-IV.
revision: Personality tests: projective (Rorschach, TAT, Rosenzweig, Szondi — ambiguous stimuli) vs objective (16PF, NEO-PI-3, EPQ-R, MBTI, MMPI, MCMI-IV — structured items). Big Five = OCEAN. MMPI = empirical keying.
confusions: Believing Rorschach has objective scoring only.

notes.t: A projective test using 10 inkblot cards. Respondents describe what they see. Administration has phases; scoring uses indices such as location, determinants and content. Scoring systems include Exner's Comprehensive System.
A projective test using ambiguous picture cards. Respondents tell stories about each picture, revealing needs, motives and conflicts. Bellak's scoring system is one approach.
A projective test presenting cartoon frustration scenes. Measures three types of aggression: extrapunitive, impunitive and intropunitive.
A projective test using photographs of people with various conditions. Based on drive theory and genetic psychology.

r: Big Five: neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness, conscientiousness
Jungian types: E/I, S/N, T/F, J/P
Edwards Personal Preference Schedule — Murray's needs

notes.t: MMPI uses empirical keying: items are included in a scale because they differentiate clinical groups, not because of face content.
UGC NET frequently asks to classify tests as projective vs objective, identify Rorschach inkblots, TAT stories, Big Five factors, and MMPI clinical scales.
